name: University of Colorado Boulder
label: CU Boulder
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Farrand Field' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Farrand Field' (way/203796978): middle (178 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/46226108: large area 'University of Colorado Boulder (Main Campus)' (2121 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Sandstone campus buildings with red tile roofs.

text.description:
The University of Colorado Boulder is the town's best-known campus, and its mix of warm sandstone, red-orange tiled roofs and mountain backdrop makes it easy to photograph. The university was founded in 1876, five months before Colorado became a state. Old Main, one of the oldest buildings, had its cornerstone laid in 1875, and the doors opened in 1877. Most of the buildings follow one look, called Tuscan Vernacular Revival, planned by the architect Charles Klauder. It uses rough sandstone walls, limestone trim and sloping tiled roofs. The stone came from quarries across the Front Range, so the buildings sit comfortably against the hills. The campus has been ranked among the most beautiful in the United States by Travel + Leisure and Condé Nast Traveler.

The classic picture is taken from the lawn of Farrand Field. Face the arch at the top of the steps and wait for someone to walk into the opening. The arch acts as a natural frame, and the Flatirons rise behind the campus. Guides suggest spring or autumn, when the trees are in bloom or changing colour. If the lawn is busy, shoot a little wider than you need and crop later. For a different view, Macky Auditorium's front steps show Old Main's red-brick tower. Varsity Bridge gives a calm scene of stone, still water and trees.
text.geographic_location: The main campus lies south of the Pearl Street Mall and east of Chautauqua Auditorium. Farrand Field is the open lawn on the campus.
text.directions_text: Head for the main campus, which lies south of the Pearl Street Mall and east of Chautauqua Auditorium. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the arch, the person and the mountains all fit. Try 2x if you want the Flatirons to look larger behind the arch. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the whole lawn, and keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Farrand Field (from the lawn, facing the arch at the top of the steps, with the Flatirons behind). A passerby or subject standing at the top of the steps, framed by the arch, with the Flatirons rising behind the campus. The campus lies to the north of you. From here the arch frames someone at the top of the steps, with the Flatirons rising behind the campus.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the arch in the middle of the picture and use the gridlines to keep its sides straight. Wait for a person to stand or walk in the opening. Leave some sky above the Flatirons so the ridge isn't cut off. For a second option, Macky Auditorium's front steps give a wider view of Old Main's red-brick tower. Varsity Bridge gives a calm lake scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the person in the arch to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and mountains keep their colour. If you are photographing a friend, portrait mode works well, but check that the arch edges are not blurred oddly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring or autumn, when the trees are in bloom or the leaves are changing.

text.access_note: The campus grounds are a working university, and the area around Old Main has reportedly been under construction in recent years, so check the official site before you go to see whether access is open.

name: Boulder Creek Path
label: Boulder Creek
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Scott Carpenter Park' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Scott Carpenter Park' (way/98568528): middle (460 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W43176659 (Boulder Creek Path): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Scenic creekside path through the middle of town.

text.description:
Boulder Creek Path is the paved trail that follows Boulder Creek through the city, and it is one of the easiest places in Boulder to get a relaxed, scenic photo. The classic picture shows the smooth creekside path in the foreground with the Flatirons, the tilted slabs of rock above the town, rising behind it. That combination of a clear leading line, trees and a big mountain backdrop is why visitors photograph it so often.

If you want something different, Eben G. Fine Park has the creek with rock structures, boulders and reflections, which suits portraits and close creekside shots. Central Park has shaded scenes of cottonwoods, stone bridges and dappled light, close to downtown.

For a phone, keep the path in the lower third of the frame so the Flatirons have room above it. Wait for a gap between cyclists and walkers so the path looks calm. Creek water can run high and fast in spring and early summer, so keep children and bags back from the banks. Conditions near the creek can change, so look at what is open when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: Boulder Creek Path runs alongside Boulder Creek through the city of Boulder, Colorado, with the Flatirons rising to the west.
text.directions_text: Boulder has no station or tram stop on this map, so start from central Boulder and head to Scott Carpenter Park. Once you are in the park, the path is easy to find beside the creek. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the path and the Flatirons together. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the rock slabs closer. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Scott Carpenter Park. The Flatirons rising behind the paved creek path, the classic Boulder backdrop for the trail. From here the Flatirons rise behind the paved creek path, which is the classic Boulder view of the trail. If the view does not line up, walk a short way along the path and try again.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the path along the lower third so it leads the eye towards the Flatirons. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, try Eben G. Fine Park for the creek, boulders and reflections, or Central Park for shaded creekside scenes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Flatirons to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and rock keep their detail. Wait for a gap in passing walkers and cyclists, or use a Live Photo to pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the rock. Spring and early summer bring fast, high water, so keep well back from the edge.

text.access_note: The path and parks are public outdoor spaces, but check current conditions locally before you go, especially at Eben G. Fine Park.

name: The Flatirons
label: The Flatirons
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chautauqua Park meadow' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Chautauqua Park' (pois).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Iconic tilted slabs of rock above the city.

text.description:
The Flatirons are a row of huge, tilted sandstone slabs on the eastern slope of Green Mountain, just above Boulder. The five numbered ones, First to Fifth, run north to south, and together they are the city's signature backdrop. The rock is roughly 290 to 296 million years old. It was pushed up and tipped on its side long ago, then uncovered by erosion. Settlers named the slabs after old-fashioned clothes irons, and once you see the sloping shapes the name makes sense.

They photograph well because the slabs are big, angled and clearly separate from the green hillside behind. The open meadow in front of the Ranger Cottage at Chautauqua Park gives you the classic postcard view. You get grasses and, in season, wildflowers in the foreground and the full line of slabs rising behind. Because the rock faces east, early morning light is the most flattering, and the slabs fall into shadow later in the day.

Keep the foreground simple, with a strip of meadow along the bottom and the rock filling the rest of the frame. If you want a different angle, NCAR gives a closer, more looming view with a striking building as a second subject, and Flatirons Vista gives a wider, calmer frame of open grassland from farther out. Check current conditions and trail access before you set off, as paths can change.
text.geographic_location: The Flatirons are near Boulder, Colorado, on the east slope of Green Mountain. The Chautauqua Park meadow, at the base of the slabs, is a classic postcard viewpoint for them.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so check current local transport options for getting to Chautauqua Park, at the base of the Flatirons. Once you are in the park, walk to the open meadow in front of the Ranger Cottage; the Flatirons are due west of there. At busy times a free weekend shuttle runs from downtown garages, so check the current details before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full line of slabs. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more meadow in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single slab or the ridge detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Chautauqua Park meadow (open meadow in front of the Ranger Cottage, facing the slabs). A green foreground with the full line of tilted sandstone slabs rising behind it, framed wide. In front of the Ranger Cottage, with the Flatirons rising to the west. From here the whole line of tilted slabs sits behind a green foreground of grass and wildflowers, which makes a wide, classic frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon of grass on the lower third line, leaving the rock to fill the upper two thirds. Crouch a little so grasses or flowers sit in the foreground, and keep your phone level so the slabs do not look as if they lean. For a different view, NCAR shows the slabs close overhead, and Flatirons Vista gives a wider, quieter frame from farther out.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rock face to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and sunlit stone keep their detail. Try a panorama if you want the whole range, and move slowly while you pan.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dawn, when the east-facing rock catches the first direct light. The slabs are in shadow by late afternoon, though some people still like the nearby viewpoints at sunset.

text.access_note: Chautauqua Park is open public parkland run by the city, but parking rules and trail access can change and some photo sessions may need a permit, so check the official site before you go.

label: Pearl Street Mall

notes: Pedestrian mall with street performers, shops and mountain views.

text.description: Pearl Street Mall is the pedestrian heart of downtown Boulder: four blocks of car-free street, running from 11th Street to 15th Street, lined with shops, restaurants and some of the city's oldest buildings. It photographs well because there is always something happening. The street is full of public art, including fountains, sculptures, a stylised map of Boulder County and small flower gardens, with tulips as the spring highlight. In summer, street performers such as musicians, jugglers and magicians add life to the frame. The Boulder County Courthouse stands in the 1300 block on the north side and makes a good solid landmark in a wider shot. The mall was built between June 1976 and August 1977 and officially dedicated on 6 August 1977. One of its designers cited a 1945 French film about busy Parisian streets and buskers as inspiration, which explains the lively, people-first feel. Because the street is open and pedestrian, you can stop and frame shots without worrying about traffic. Look for a long view down the street for atmosphere, then move closer for details: a fountain, a flowerbed, a performer in action. Please ask before filming or photographing performers up close, and keep clear of the middle of the walkway so people can pass.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of downtown Boulder, in the western part of the city, on Pearl Street between 11th Street and 15th Street. The Boulder County Courthouse sits on the north side of the 1300 block.
text.directions_text: Walk east along the street and you are in the pedestrian area. The phone icon on the map is about 180 m west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long street view and public art, then switch to the default lens (1x) for people and shopfronts. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for performers and details from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 180 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here you can capture the street running away from you, with the buildings on both sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with the centre or a third of the frame so the buildings lead the eye. Include a sculpture, a flowerbed or a few passers-by in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For close-ups of a sculpture or fountain, try portrait mode. Try a Live Photo when a performer is mid-act.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the street to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and building highlights keep their detail. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring for the tulips and summer for street performers. Late afternoon into evening gives warm light and a livelier crowd, and the shop and restaurant lights come on.

text.access_note: This is an open public pedestrian street, but check the official site before you go for any events or closures.

text.description: Hotel Boulderado stands at the corner of 13th and Spruce Street in downtown Boulder, Colorado. It is a historic hotel with a long, solid frontage, and it makes a good, uncomplicated street photo of the town's early twentieth-century character. It opened on New Year's Day 1909, after a gala ball the night before. It was designed by the local architects William Redding, Floyd Redding and James Cowie of Redding & Sons, who took inspiration from Italian Renaissance and Spanish Colonial Revival styles. That mix explains the classic look of the building, which suits a wide, straight-on shot. Inside, the stained-glass ceiling of the lobby is the best-known feature. It was designed to echo the ceiling of San Francisco's Palace Hotel. The original 1908 Otis elevator is still in use, and the first guest register is on display in the main lobby. The hotel was added to Historic Hotels of America in 1996. For a phone photo, the main job is fitting the building in without tilting the camera. Keep your phone upright and use the gridlines so the walls stay straight. Then move closer for details such as windows, signs and brickwork. If you want to photograph inside, check the official site before you go and be polite to guests and staff.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Boulder, on the corner of 13th Street and Spruce Street, in the town's central area.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown Boulder and head for the corner of 13th and Spruce Street. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you will be standing close to a long building. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as upper windows and signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. You will be close, so face the hotel and take a step or two back if the whole frontage doesn't fit.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the building with a vertical line, holding the phone level and upright to keep the walls from leaning. Try one wide shot with the full frontage, then a tighter one on the corner and the entrance. If you go in, the stained-glass lobby ceiling is worth a photo pointing upwards, subject to the hotel's rules.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it doesn't turn white. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually looks best on a building like this. At dusk, lit windows and entrance make a warm night-mode shot.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but the hotel is a working business, so check the official site before you go if you want to take photos inside.

name: Folsom Field
label: Folsom Field
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Monarch of the Plains' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Monarch of the Plains' (node/593993851): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18555106: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Folsom Field' (289 m across).
notes: Buffaloes football stadium with the Flatirons behind it.

text.description:
Folsom Field is the University of Colorado's football stadium, and it sits on the University of Colorado campus in Boulder. The best phone photo here is not of the stadium alone. Start at the Monarch of the Plains, the bronze buffalo statue outside Gate 1 on the Balch Fieldhouse courtyard side. It gives you a strong foreground subject, with the stadium entrance and campus buildings behind it. Visitors also come for the statue's Ralphie association, and it is a regular stop on campus tours.

The stadium opened in 1924 as Colorado Stadium and was renamed Folsom Field in 1944, after former head coach Fred Folsom. It is horseshoe-shaped and opens to the north. It stands at 5,360 feet (1,635 m), more than a mile above sea level. Its brick facades and the green field are worth a shot, and a second option is the outside of the east side, where the Flatirons and foothills rise behind the stands.

Photographing the statue is straightforward. Stand a few steps back so the buffalo fills the lower part of the frame and the entrance sits behind it. If people are walking past, wait a moment for a clear gap. On match days and event days the area is busy, so allow extra time and be patient with the crowds.
text.geographic_location: Folsom Field is on the University of Colorado campus in Boulder. Balch Fieldhouse stands on its west side, and the Monarch of the Plains statue is in the courtyard outside Gate 1.
text.directions_text: Head for the University of Colorado campus in Boulder. Make for Balch Fieldhouse and the courtyard outside Gate 1, where the Monarch of the Plains statue stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the buffalo statue with the entrance behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want more of the stadium's brick frontage, and use 2x or more to pick out details such as the bronze figure or the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (at the bronze buffalo statue near the Folsom Field entrance, outside Gate 1 on the Balch Fieldhouse courtyard side). The bronze buffalo statue in the foreground with the stadium entrance and campus buildings behind it. From here the photo shows the statue in the foreground, with the stadium entrance and campus buildings behind it. The main part of Folsom Field lies to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the buffalo on one third line, with the entrance filling the rest of the frame. Crouch slightly so the statue stands out against the buildings. For a second picture, walk round to the outside of the stadium's east side and shoot the brick facades with the Flatirons and foothills behind the stands. Views from inside the stands are generally for event days only, so check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the bronze keeps its detail. Portrait mode can work on the buffalo if you stand fairly close, but check the edges of the statue in the result.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the bronze and fewer people in the courtyard. Avoid event days if you want a clear view of the statue.

text.access_note: The statue stands outside the stadium and is free to photograph, but the stadium itself is generally open only for events, so check the official site before you go.

name: Colorado Chautauqua
label: Chautauqua Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ranger Cottage' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ranger Cottage' (way/222216436): middle (20 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.

notes: Historic park and cottages at the foot of the Flatirons.

text.description: Colorado Chautauqua is a historic gathering ground at the foot of the Flatirons, on the southern edge of Boulder. It began in 1898 as a summer school and lecture series, and it is still running today as a year-round programme of talks, concerts and silent films. The whole 40-acre site, with its historic cottages, dining hall and the 1898 auditorium, was made a National Historic Landmark in 2006. For photographers the appeal is the setting: old buildings and open green lawns with the tilted sandstone slabs of the Flatirons rising straight behind them. Most visitors point their phones at the rocks rather than the buildings, and the best-known spot is the meadow in front of Ranger Cottage, where the Flatirons loom almost directly overhead. A second good option is Chautauqua Meadow itself, where grasses and wildflowers can fill the foreground. If you want a longer view back over the green and the auditorium roofs, the Walter Orr Roberts Weather Trail looks north along the slabs. The grounds and the adjoining park are open to the public with no entry fee, so you can wander and try several angles. Allow a few minutes to walk between the meadow and the main cluster of historic buildings.
text.geographic_location: Colorado Chautauqua sits on the southern edge of Boulder, just south of Baseline Road, with Boulder Mountain Parks to the south and west, and the Flatirons close by.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from central Boulder and head south towards Baseline Road. The Chautauqua grounds are on the southern edge of Boulder. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the Flatirons and the meadow together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the rock faces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Ranger Cottage (meadow in front of the cottage). The Flatirons looming directly overhead from the meadow in front of the historic Ranger Cottage. For the best-known view of the Flatirons, the recommended viewpoint is the meadow in front of Ranger Cottage, where the rocks loom almost directly overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. Hold the phone low so the meadow grass fills the bottom of the frame, with the rock slabs above. For a different view, Chautauqua Meadow shows the Flatirons rising behind open grass and wildflowers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rocks to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the sandstone. With the ultra-wide, keep your fingers clear of the edges of the lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, when the rocks catch the first light.

text.access_note: The Chautauqua grounds and the adjoining park are open to the public without an entry fee, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit an event or building.

name: Flagstaff Mountain
label: Flagstaff Mountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Panorama Point' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Panorama Point' (way/996186614): middle (51 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/358913110: the OpenStreetMap point 'Flagstaff Mountain'.
notes: Mountain road and summit with wide views over Boulder.

text.description: Flagstaff Mountain is the foothill that rises straight up from the western edge of Boulder, part of Boulder Mountain Park in the Flatirons region on the eastern flank of the Front Range. Its summit stands at 6,983 feet (2,128 m). For photographs, the mountain is mostly a place to look out from rather than something to shoot head-on. Panorama Point, the first pullout on the right going up Flagstaff Road from Baseline Road, is the easy, classic overlook. From here Boulder and the eastern plains spread out below you, with a clear view and space to stop and take your time. It is a popular spot at sunrise and sunset, when the town and plains pick up softer colour. Other overlooks on the mountain give different views. Lost Gulch Overlook shows rugged rock and forested foothills with the Indian Peaks and Continental Divide beyond. Realization Point shows layered foothills and the Flatirons in front of Boulder. On your phone, start wide to take in the whole sweep of the plains, then zoom in for details such as streets and rooftops. Allow for the weather: cloud can hide the view, and snow can close trails in winter. Flagstaff Summit Road is seasonal and closes in the evening, so don't plan on staying out until full dark.
text.geographic_location: Flagstaff Mountain sits on the western edge of Boulder, inside Boulder Mountain Park, above the Baseline Road end of town. Panorama Point is the first pullout on Flagstaff Road, looking out over the city.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed nearby. Flagstaff Road runs up from Baseline Road, and Panorama Point is the first pullout on the right. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view over Boulder, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of the plains. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details in the town below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Panorama Point (first pullout on the right going up Flagstaff Road from Baseline Road). Boulder and the eastern plains spread out below, with room to set up a tripod for sunrise or sunset. The first pullout on the right going up Flagstaff Road from Baseline Road. From here you look out over Boulder and the eastern plains spread below, with the mountain's summit to the west, behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the town in the lower half and plenty of sky above. Tap the screen on the town to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little at sunset so the sky keeps its colour. If you want a different view, Lost Gulch Overlook shows rugged rock and foothills with the Indian Peaks beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Try panorama mode held steady, moving slowly from left to right, for the wide plains. As the light fades, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep it sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset are the best times. Check the road gate times first, because the summit road closes in the evening.

text.access_note: Flagstaff Summit Road is seasonal and closes in the evening, and vehicles not registered in Boulder County may need a parking permit or fee, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Center for Atmospheric Research
label: NCAR Mesa Lab
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mesa Trail' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mesa Trail' (way/129859889): point nearest the subject (414 m long).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: I. M. Pei-designed lab set against the mountains.

text.description:
The National Center for Atmospheric Research is Boulder's big climate and weather laboratory, founded in 1960 and still headquartered here at its Mesa Laboratory. It is sponsored by the National Science Foundation and managed by the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research. The building is the main draw for photographers: I.M. Pei's angular sandstone towers sit on a mesa with the Flatirons and open foothills behind them. That gives you strong shapes, warm stone and a big sky in one frame.

From here you get a quieter, wilder view than the usual front-of-building shot. Bear Canyon and Bear Peak rise to the south, with grassland and pines in the foreground, and in spring there can be wildflowers at your feet. You reach it by following the NCAR trail past a large green water tank.

For a classic building picture, the NCAR Mesa Laboratory itself is the alternative, especially around sunrise or sunset. The Walter Orr Roberts Weather Trail, close to the laboratory, gives framed views of the Flatirons and Bear Peak over ponderosa pines. Wear proper shoes, bring water, and check conditions first: summer thunderstorms and snow can affect access, and the lab's public access can change.
text.geographic_location: On a mesa below the foothills, with the Flatirons rising just behind the laboratory. The Mesa Trail viewpoint lies about 1 km to the north-west of the building.
text.directions_text: Head for the Mesa Laboratory, which sits on a mesa below the foothills. There is no public transport stop at the spot, so check parking and access before you go. The subject lies to the south-east of it, about 1 km away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of foothills, grass and pines. Use the default lens (1x) for a balanced view of Bear Peak, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the laboratory and the Flatirons closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mesa Trail (Vista on the trail west of the laboratory, reached by following the NCAR trail past a large green water tank; the blog gives coordinates about 39.9774, -105.2814). A quieter, wilder foothills vista with Bear Canyon and Bear Peak to the south and grassland and pines in the foreground. From here the view looks south to Bear Canyon and Bear Peak, with grassland and pines in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Include some grass or pine branches in the bottom of the frame to give depth. Keep Bear Peak off-centre. For a classic building shot, the NCAR Mesa Laboratory itself shows the sandstone towers with the Flatirons behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountains to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If the building turns very dark against a bright sky, tap on the stone and then lower the exposure slightly. Panorama mode works well for the full foothills sweep if you hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the hills and the building. Spring is the time to look for wildflowers.

text.access_note: Check that the trail is open and what the access rules are before you go. The laboratory itself is a working research site, so check the official site for public access, parking and trail conditions.

name: Dushanbe Teahouse
label: Dushanbe Tea House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Central Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Central Park' (way/533289100): middle (235 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/207394089: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Boulder Dushanbe Tea House' (38 m across).
notes: Ornately hand-painted teahouse gifted by Boulder's sister city Dushanbe.

text.description:
The Dushanbe Teahouse is one of Boulder's most unusual buildings, and it photographs well because it looks nothing like its neighbours. It was a gift to Boulder from its sister city, Dushanbe in Tajikistan, in 1987. Forty Tajik artisans spent about two years making it by hand, then took it apart and packed it into roughly 200 crates for the journey. It took years to raise the money to put it up, and it finally opened to the public in 1998. Outside, eight ceramic panels show a 'Tree of life' pattern. The teahouse also sits beside a small brook that runs off Boulder Creek, with a rose garden in its grounds.

From the park opposite you can fit the whole colourful front of the building into one frame, with the park lawn or snow in the foreground. That wide view shows the teahouse in its setting. Then walk over to the entrance for a second, closer picture of the ceramic panels, framed by trellises, vines and rose bushes. Roses and the garden are seasonal, so the entry looks greenest in the warmer months. The Boulder Creek Path runs right past the property if you want a quieter side-on view. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the building's edges stay straight.
text.geographic_location: The teahouse stands beside a brook off Boulder Creek, close to the park in central Boulder (the park may now be labelled Boulder Creek Park on the map).
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head into central Boulder and make your way to the park and the Boulder Creek Path area. Walk about 68 m north-east towards the front of the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole front of the teahouse from the park. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the park and sky, and keep the building away from the edges of the frame to avoid stretching. Use 2x for the tile panels if your phone has it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Central Park (across the street from the teahouse, facing its front). The teahouse seen from the park side, with its colorful exterior and the snowy or green park in the foreground. Facing the front of the teahouse. From here you see the colourful exterior with the green or snowy park in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the front of the building up with them so the walls stand straight. Leave some lawn or snow at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of place. For an alternative, go to the entrance and take a close shot of one of the eight blue ceramic panels, framed by trellis, vines and roses.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the colours of the exterior stay rich. In snow, slide the exposure up slightly so the white doesn't look grey.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the colours best. Visit in the warmer months if you want the rose beds and entry garden at their fullest.

text.access_note: The park and the Boulder Creek Path are public open space, but the teahouse is a working restaurant, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.

name: Boulder Theater
label: Boulder Theater
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Boulder Theater' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q132746180: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Art Deco theater with a classic marquee sign.

text.description:
Boulder Theater is a music venue on 14th Street, just off Pearl Street, and its front is the part most visitors photograph. The art deco facade and the lit marquee make a strong, simple subject: one building, one clear sign, and a street to frame it against. It looks its best at dusk, when the lights come on and the marquee glows against the darkening sky.

The building opened in 1906 as the Curran Opera House. In 1936 it became a cinema and was renamed the Boulder Theater, and its art deco look was inspired by the nearby Boulder courthouse. In 1979 the facade and marquee came under a historic easement held by Historic Boulder, to protect the artwork and design. After closing in 1983 it reopened in 1988 following a big renovation, and it still hosts live acts today.

For a phone photo, stand on the street in front and aim at the marquee. The marquee is the feature to keep in the frame, so leave a little space above it for the sign and the sky. Keep your gridlines on so the vertical lines of the facade stay straight. Pedestrians and passing cars are likely on this street, so be patient and take a few frames to get a clean one. If you want a picture of the whole building, step back across the street, as long as it is safe to do so.
text.geographic_location: Boulder Theater is in central Boulder, on 14th Street about half a block off Pearl Street. It stands a short distance from the Boulder courthouse, which inspired its art deco design.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from central Boulder and the Pearl Street area, then head to 14th Street, about half a block away. The phone icon on the map is right in front of the building, so you do not need to walk any further. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and marquee. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole front in. Use 2x if you want to focus on the marquee lettering alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is right where you are standing, so the photo shows the lit marquee and art deco front against the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the marquee in the upper-middle of the frame, with the facade filling the rest. Turn on gridlines and keep them level with the building's lines. Tilt the phone slightly upward only as much as you need, because the vertical lines will lean inwards if you tilt too far. Include a little of the street or pavement to give a sense of place.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the marquee to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not blow out to white. At dusk or after dark, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or after dark, when the marquee lights are on and the facade is lit.

text.access_note: The front of the theatre can be photographed from the public street; if you want to go inside, check the official site before you go.

name: Fox Theatre
label: Fox Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '1135 13th St' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'College Ave & 13th St' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/200802355: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fox Theatre' (41 m across).
notes: Well-known music venue on The Hill.

text.description: The Fox Theatre is a live music venue on The Hill, Boulder's busy district of restaurants, bars and shops just across the street from the University of Colorado campus. It sits on 13th Street beside the Tulagi's building. From the street it is the lettering and the marquee that catch the eye. The marquee and the Fox sign are both original, left over from the days when the building was a cinema. The cinema opened in 1961, and when the old building was opened up in the early 1990s, work revealed that its roots go back to 1926. The venue first opened its doors on 6 March 1992 and can seat just over 600 people. It has hosted a long list of well-known touring and local acts, and it marked its 30th anniversary in 2022. That mix of old signage, a lively street and a real music-venue feel makes for a good, characterful travel photo. The simplest picture is a straight-on view of the front, with the sign and entrance filling the frame. Walk up to the facade, stand where the whole front fits, keep your phone upright so the walls stay straight, and wait a moment for people to walk out of the shot. The Hill is a busy street, so expect passers-by, and crowds or sidewalk activity can block the view. A second option is to move along 13th Street and photograph the facade as part of the street scene.
text.geographic_location: The Fox Theatre is on 13th Street in The Hill, Boulder's commercial, restaurant and bar district, next to the Tulagi's building and across the street from the University of Colorado campus.
text.directions_text: Head for 13th Street on The Hill, the district just across from the University of Colorado campus. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural, straight-on view of the front. If the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back far enough, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close-up of the sign or marquee.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (directly in front of the street-facing facade). The Fox Theatre's front facade and entrance straight on from the sidewalk across or in front of the building. Face north-west and walk toward the building. For the straight-on frontal view, cross to the pavement in front of 1135 13th St, directly facing the street-facing facade, and shoot the building from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the front does not lean. Put the sign and marquee in the upper half of the frame, with the entrance below. If the frontal view is blocked, an alternative is to walk along 13th Street and take a wider shot along the street, with the Fox's facade as one building on the block.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lettering stays sharp and does not wash out against the sky. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest straight-on view of the facade. If the sign is lit, evening may add colour, but crowds or sidewalk activity can block the view.

text.access_note: The front of the building faces the street, but it is a working live-music venue, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Boulder County Courthouse
label: County Courthouse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pearl Street' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Pearl Street and 14th Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q115805796: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neoclassical courthouse at the east end of the Pearl Street Mall.

text.description:
The Boulder County Courthouse stands on Pearl Street, along the pedestrian mall in downtown Boulder. It is a five-storey building with strong vertical lines, a tower and very little decoration. The style is called WPA Moderne, a restrained form of Art Deco. Architect Glen H. Huntington designed it, and it went up in 1933 on the site of the 1882 courthouse, which burned down in 1932. The courts have since moved out, but it is still the seat of county government.

The building also has a place in civil rights history. In 1975 the county clerk, Clela Rorex, issued marriage licences to six same-sex couples here, among the first in the United States. The courthouse became a National Historic Landmark in 2024. It is also part of the Downtown Boulder Historic District.

The Flatirons may show behind the downtown blocks, but check on the day. For a second view, try the front lawn side, where the limestone facade sits behind the grass with the mall beside it. Keep to public ground. This is a working government building, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or photograph the grounds closely.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Boulder, on Pearl Street beside the pedestrian mall, in the Downtown Boulder Historic District.
text.directions_text: The courthouse is 67 m to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the courthouse along the street. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the tower will not fit, or if you want more street in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower and facade lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Pearl Street and 14th Street (west end of the mall, looking east down the 1300 block). The courthouse along the pedestrian mall with the Flatirons rising to the west behind the downtown blocks. From here the courthouse sits along Pearl Street. The Flatirons may show behind the downtown blocks, but check on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn towards the courthouse (south-west) and let the street lead the eye to it. Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the tower or the building's edge so the stonework stays upright. As an alternative, walk round to the front lawn side and shoot the limestone facade with the grass in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the stone to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white. If you raise the phone to fit the tower in, keep it level so the vertical lines do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset on a clear evening, when the low light warms the stone and, if the Flatirons show behind the downtown blocks, may colour them too.

text.access_note: The mall and the street are open public space, but the courthouse is a working county government building, so check the official site before you go for access to the building and grounds.
